design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of one survey wave (January to June 2021) of the Happiness and Health Study, a cohort first recruited in ninth grade at ten Los Angeles high schools in 2013; 1312 respondents aged 21 to 24 who drank in the past 30 days. Exposure: ever having used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), yes or no. Outcomes: a modified AUDIT score (0 to 40), drinking days, binge-drinking days, drinks per drinking day, and a count of seven alcohol problems; linear and negative binomial regressions, unadjusted and adjusted for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms; the reverse direction in a supplement.
can_establish: How many young adults in this Southern California cohort had used, heard of, or believed in hangover remedy pills in 2021, and whether those who had used them reported more drinking problems and heavier drinking than those who had not, at one point in time.
cannot_establish: Whether remedy pills lead people to drink more, or heavier drinking leads people to try remedies (the direction is unknown and both are plausible, as the authors say); whether the pills work or are safe (not studied); and anything about regular or recent use, or about remedies other than pills (the single item asked about ever-use of pills).

sample.recruitment: Cohort originally recruited from ninth graders at ten high schools in Los Angeles in 2013 and surveyed repeatedly; this analysis uses the 2021 wave.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents to the 2021 wave who reported drinking alcohol in the past 30 days and answered the remedy question.
sample.demographics: Mean age 21.8 (SD 0.4); 61.4% women, 34.8% men, 3.8% another gender identity; 25.0% non-heterosexual; 47.4% Hispanic or Latino, 18.0% white, 15.7% Asian, 18.9% another race or ethnicity; 63.7% enrolled in a degree programme, 68.6% in paid work, 60.7% not living comfortably financially; mean CES-D-10 depression score 9.9 (SD 6.2).
sample.attrition: Not reported for the cohort: the number originally recruited and retained to 2021 is not given in this paper. Covariates were missing for 158 respondents (12.0%) and multiply imputed.
sample.selection_effects: One region and one school-based cohort, with unknown attrition since 2013; past-30-day drinkers only; only 42 respondents had used remedy pills, which limits precision and generalization.

exposure.measurement: One self-report item: ever used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), yes or no. Awareness (ever heard of remedy pills to prevent hangovers) and belief (do you feel they work) were single yes/no items.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: no information on how often, how recently, which product or why.

comparison.controls: Past-30-day drinkers in the same survey who had never used hangover remedy pills.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age, gender and sexual identity, race and ethnicity, enrolment, employment, financial situation and depressive symptoms; the problem-count model was further adjusted for drinking frequency, binge frequency and drinks per drinking day.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality traits such as sensation seeking, peer drinking, earlier drinking history from the cohort's own previous waves, and hangover frequency or severity were not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: A modified AUDIT (10 items, 0 to 40), with the first three consumption items converted from the survey's own response options (Supplemental Table S1, not read); past-30-day drinking days, binge-drinking days (standard sex-specific definition) and drinks per typical drinking day, recoded from ranges to midpoints; a past-year count of seven alcohol problems, called an AUD symptom count.
outcomes.validity_norms: The AUDIT is a validated screening instrument; the consumption items were converted rather than asked as in the AUDIT. The seven items of the problem count (unable to stop, failing expectations, morning drinking, guilt, blackouts, injury, others' concern) are the AUDIT's problem items, not DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder.
outcomes.operationalization: Differences in modified AUDIT score (unstandardized B) and incidence rate ratios for the counts, the ever-use group against the never-use group.

analysis.effect_sizes: Ever-use group against never-use group: modified AUDIT 7.7 (SD 4.7) against 5.4 (4.7), adjusted B = 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76), unadjusted 2.45 (0.96 to 3.93); drinks per typical drinking day, adjusted IRR 1.24 (1.02 to 1.49); alcohol problem count 1.7 against 0.9, adjusted IRR 1.86 (1.18 to 3.02), after also adjusting for drinking frequency and intensity; drinking days 6.4 against 5.6, adjusted IRR 1.19 (0.94 to 1.51), and binge days 2.6 against 2.1, adjusted IRR 1.40 (0.91 to 2.23), both not significant. Prevalence: 3.2% had ever used remedy pills (42 of 1312), 18.9% had heard of them, 8.6% believed they work.
analysis.covariates: Age, gender identity, sexual identity, race and ethnicity, enrolment in a degree programme, paid employment, financial situation and CES-D-10 depressive symptoms; missing covariates handled by multiple imputation.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the authors call the study exploratory.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five outcomes are reported with intervals; the reverse-direction analyses are in a supplement that was not read.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the authors note reduced power from the small number of people who had used remedy pills (42).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2021, 42 of 1312 young adult drinkers in a Los Angeles cohort (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills. Compared with those who had not, they scored about 2.3 points higher on a 0 to 40 alcohol problem scale, drank about a quarter more drinks per drinking day, and reported almost twice as many alcohol problems, but did not drink on detectably more days or binge on more days. About one in five had heard of remedy pills and fewer than one in ten believed they work.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state an association and call for scientific and regulatory attention, which is consistent with the data, and the Limitations state plainly that causal interpretation is not possible. Gaps: (1) the Discussion speculates that remedy beliefs lead young adults to drink more and raises concern that remedy marketing could increase drinking, which a single cross-sectional association involving 42 people who had used the pills cannot support, as the authors partly acknowledge; (2) the problem count is called an AUD symptom count, although its items are the AUDIT's problem items rather than diagnostic criteria; (3) the Discussion recommends strategies (pacing, alternating with non-alcoholic drinks, medical evaluation for frequent hangovers) that this study did not examine.

timeline.event: Verster et al. review of 82 hangover remedy products sold on a US retail website (cited by the authors for product ingredients and marketing claims; not read here).
This study: by the authors' account the first to examine remedy use against drinking patterns and alcohol problems.

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional association in one cohort; no longitudinal study has tested whether remedy use comes before heavier drinking or follows it.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products (U54CA180905), National Cancer Institute (R01CA229617) and National Institute on Drug Abuse (K24DA048160).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the University of Southern California; the cohort is run by the senior author's group.

what_would_settle_it: A longitudinal study in the same or a similar cohort measuring remedy use (type, frequency, reasons) and drinking at several waves, testing whether starting remedy use is followed by heavier drinking or follows it, with adjustment for earlier drinking, hangover frequency and sensation seeking.

domains.note: Adjusted only for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms; earlier drinking, hangover frequency, personality and peers were not, and heavier drinking may itself lead to remedy use.
One self-report item on ever using remedy pills, with one example product; no recency, frequency or product information.
A school-based cohort with unreported attrition since 2013, restricted to past-30-day drinkers.
Not applicable to a single survey.
17 excluded for a missing exposure; covariates missing for 12% and multiply imputed.
Self-reported drinking and problems, recoded from response ranges; consumption items converted to the AUDIT scale.
Exploratory and not registered, but all planned outcomes are reported with intervals, including null ones.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For any causal reading (remedy use leading to heavier drinking, or the reverse) the risk of bias is high: the direction is unknown and important confounders were not measured. For the association as described, the main limits are a single crude exposure item and only 42 people who had used the pills. The card may be cited for the prevalence of remedy-pill use, awareness and belief in this cohort, and for the association of ever-use with more drinks per drinking day and more alcohol problems; not for any effect of remedies on drinking.

key_findings.finding: Of 1312 past-30-day drinkers aged 21 to 24 in 2021, 42 (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills, 248 (18.9%) had heard of them, and 110 (8.6%) believed they work.
The ever-use group scored higher on the modified AUDIT (7.7, SD 4.7, against 5.4, SD 4.7); adjusted difference B = 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76) on a 0 to 40 scale.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Alcohol use problem score; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The ever-use group drank more per typical drinking day (about a quarter more; adjusted IRR 1.24, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.49) and reported more alcohol problems (1.7 against 0.9 of 7; adjusted IRR 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02, also adjusted for drinking frequency and intensity).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, drinks per typical drinking day and Past Year AUD symptom count rows; Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ever-use was not detectably associated with the number of drinking days (6.4 against 5.6; adjusted IRR 1.19, 0.94 to 1.51) or binge-drinking days (2.6 against 2.1; adjusted IRR 1.40, 0.91 to 2.23).
In the reverse direction, higher problem scores, more drinks per drinking day and more alcohol problems were associated with higher odds of ever having used remedy pills.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (last sentence); Supplemental Table S2 (not read)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that causal interpretation is not possible, that the exposure item cannot separate recent from past or occasional from regular use, and that the small number of people who had used the pills limits power and generalizability.

reporting_issues.issue: The unadjusted AUDIT difference is marked with three asterisks, a symbol the table footnote does not define (it defines one and two); its interval (0.96 to 3.93) corresponds to p of about 0.001 (editors' calculation), not clearly below 0.001.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 and its notes
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the adjusted estimate (two asterisks, p about 0.002) is the one to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The seven-item count called an AUD symptom count consists of the AUDIT's problem items (unable to stop, failing expectations, morning drinking, guilt, blackouts, injury, others' concern), not DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Alcohol use problems; Table 2, footnote d
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say alcohol-related problems, not symptoms of alcohol use disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportion of missing covariate data is printed as 'n = 158.12.0%'.
The original size of the cohort and its retention to the 2021 wave are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study design and participants
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection by attrition cannot be judged from this paper.
